subject: Asking rents fell 3.6%. In-place rents still rose 2.2%
bodyMarkdown:
Statistics Canada reported yesterday that the average asking rent for a two-bedroom apartment fell again in the spring. If you rent anywhere near Toronto, the question worth asking is whether your own rent is falling too, and for most tenants it is not.

## What the release said

The number is $2,130 a month, averaged across all census metropolitan areas in the second quarter, down $20 from the first quarter and down 3.6 per cent, or about $80, from a year earlier. That is the **asking rent**, the price a landlord lists a vacant unit at, so it describes the market for people signing a new lease and nobody else. Vancouver is still the most expensive place to sign one at $3,030. Toronto came in at $2,650, down from $2,660 in the first quarter, which is a rounding error dressed up as relief. The steepest annual drops were in Abbotsford-Mission and Calgary at 6.4 per cent each, Montreal at 5.2 and Vancouver at 4.1. Halifax went the other way and now sits at $2,400, the fourth most expensive market in the country.

## The rent people actually pay

Now the other half of the picture. Storeys, citing Yardi's national multifamily report, put the average **in-place rent**, what tenants already living somewhere are paying, at $1,774 in the second quarter, up $6 on the quarter and 2.2 per cent on the year. The two figures are not directly comparable (in-place covers every unit size, the Statistics Canada number is two-bedrooms only), so watch the directions rather than the gap. New leases are getting cheaper while renewals keep getting more expensive, and almost all the growth in what landlords collect now comes from people who stayed put. Turnover rose to 26.2 per cent nationally from 24.2 a year earlier. I read that as tenants doing the arithmetic and moving, which for two years was the expensive choice.

## Why the market loosened

Supply, mostly. BMO Capital Markets, working from Statistics Canada data, found that purpose-built rentals made up 50.6 per cent of Canadian housing starts in 2025, 113,200 apartment starts, the first year they passed half. Add slower population growth from lower immigration targets and you get a vacancy rate that climbed for nine straight quarters. In the second quarter it fell 40 basis points to 4.7 per cent, its first drop in that run, though it is still above the 4.1 per cent of a year earlier. Halifax at 2.4 per cent and Winnipeg at 2.8 are the tightest markets, Calgary at 6.8 and Edmonton at 5.8 the loosest. So the window where a renter holds some leverage is real, and it has already started to close.

## The takeaway

If your lease is up in the next six months, price a comparable unit before you sign a renewal, because the listed price may now be under what you are already paying. Landlords are advertising down and renewing up, and only one of those numbers ends up on your lease. Statistics Canada's July inflation report, released August 17, put headline CPI at 3.0 per cent, so rent is pulling inflation down while tariffs push it up, which is part of why the Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent on September 2. I am watching third-quarter vacancy: if it falls again, yesterday's numbers were close to the best deal renters are going to see.
